match.reason: No single bank point covers all three structures (sole trader, partnership and company) with the liability comparison; the three Year 7 cards each cover only one structure, so the new point is broader than any of them, and the Year 11 card is at a greater depth.

draft.title: Business ownership structures
card: Sole trader
a business owned and run by one person. The owner keeps the profit, and the business is not a separate legal entity from them.
Partnership
a business owned by two or more people who share the work, the profit and the risk.
Company
a separate legal entity, which means the law treats it as its own person. It is owned by shareholders, who each own a share of it.
If a sole trader or partnership fails, the owners can lose their own assets, such as savings or a car, to pay its debts.
draft.remember: Sole trader: one owner. Partnership: two or more. Company: shareholders own a separate legal entity.

opts: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders
A business owned and run by one person
A business owned by two or more people who share risk
A business whose owners lose their own assets if it fails
a.why: A company is its own legal entity, and shareholders own it. The option about two or more people sharing risk describes a partnership, which is not a separate legal entity.
a.clue: Think about who the law treats as the business.

b.q: Tariq and Lena run a bike repair shop in Bendigo. They own it together, and the shop is not a separate legal entity. The shop fails and owes money. What could happen?
opts: Tariq and Lena could lose their own assets
Only the shop's own assets could be used to pay
Shareholders would lose the shares they own
Tariq and Lena would not be affected at all
b.why: Two owners with no separate legal entity make this a partnership. Its owners can lose their own assets to pay its debts. Only the shop's assets being at risk is tempting, but that fits a company, which the card does not describe here.
b.clue: Work out the structure first, then think about whose assets are at risk.

a.best: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders

b.best: Tariq and Lena could lose their own assets

problems.detail: Why (b) says the 'only the shop's assets' option 'fits a company, which the card does not describe here'. This is confusing because the card does describe companies. It also leans on limited liability, which the card never states, so students may be unsure what the card teaches.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate and each has one clear answer. Why (b) is confusingly worded: it ties 'only the shop's assets' to companies while saying the card does not describe this, and the card never teaches limited liability.
